core: What a learning objective is: a claim about what the learner will be able to do, stated so a second party could check it
How an objective differs from a goal, from a classroom activity, and from an externally adopted standard
Mager's three components (performance, conditions, criterion) and the ABCD elaboration that adds audience
The argument against over-specification: when conditions and degree earn their place and when they manufacture false precision
Observable versus unobservable verbs, and why 'understand' and 'appreciate' fail as operative verbs
Bloom's taxonomy: the 1956 committee and its purpose, the 2001 Anderson & Krathwohl revision, the six cognitive process categories and the four knowledge types
Honest treatment of the cumulative-hierarchy assumption and of the limits of verb lists
Constructive alignment: objective to instruction to assessment (Biggs)
Grain size: course-level, unit-level and lesson-level objectives
Eisner's critique of behavioural objectives and the expressive objective as an alternative form
supporting: The affective domain handbook (Krathwohl, Bloom & Masia, 1964) and the fact that the originating group never published a psychomotor taxonomy
The Taxonomy Table as an alignment-checking device
The distinction between content coverage and opportunity to learn

claims.claim: A learning objective states what the learner will be able to do after instruction, in terms someone else could check; the NYSED formulation requires student performance, the conditions of performance, and a criterion of acceptable accuracy, which is the three-part structure Mager set out in 1962.

Verbs naming internal states - 'learn', 'understand', 'become familiar with' - fail as operative verbs in an objective because a teacher cannot observe a student understanding; acceptable verbs name a measurable action such as defining, listing, or installing.

A fixed percentage criterion is not always appropriate: NYSED explicitly warns that a 70 percent accuracy standard is unacceptable for tasks such as drawing blood or installing a network card, and that standards like 'to the satisfaction of the instructor' are unusable. Conditions may be omitted where they follow from the instruction itself.

The 1956 Taxonomy of Educational Objectives, Handbook I: Cognitive Domain was produced by a committee - Bloom as editor with Engelhart, Furst, Hill and Krathwohl - drawn from measurement specialists who met about twice a year from 1949; Bloom, then associate director of the University of Chicago Board of Examinations, initiated it to reduce the labour of preparing annual comprehensive examinations.

The affective domain was published separately as Handbook II by Krathwohl, Bloom and Masia in 1964, and the originating group never published a psychomotor taxonomy; the psychomotor taxonomies in circulation were produced independently by Simpson (1966), Dave (1970) and Harrow (1972).

The 2001 revision edited by Anderson and Krathwohl restates the six cognitive categories as verbs - remember, understand, apply, analyze, evaluate, create - renaming Synthesis as Create and moving it to the top, and adds a second Knowledge dimension of factual, conceptual, procedural and metacognitive knowledge, crossed with the cognitive processes in a Taxonomy Table.

The original taxonomy's cumulative hierarchy was an assumption the committee stated rather than a finding it demonstrated, and the 2001 revision explicitly relaxed the requirement of a strict hierarchy so the categories may overlap - Krathwohl's own example is that Explaining, within Understand, is more cognitively complex than Executing, within Apply.

Empirical testing of the revised taxonomy's internal assumptions across 940 assessment items found that the knowledge-type and cognitive-process dimensions are related rather than independent, and found no clear relationship between question prompt words, including action verbs, and the cognitive process actually embedded in the item; the authors conclude that action verbs alone are not sufficient to classify an objective's level.

A statement of a learning objective contains a verb and an object: the verb refers to the intended cognitive process and the object describes the knowledge the student is expected to acquire or construct.

Constructive alignment, named by Biggs in 1996, requires that objectives be derived as performances at a suitably high cognitive level, that teaching and learning activities be chosen because they are judged to elicit those performances, and that assessment report the same performances.

Alignment questions differ depending on where the analysis starts: content coverage asks whether what is being taught is being tested, opportunity to learn asks whether what is being tested has been taught, and curricular alignment concerns the relationship between objectives and assessments.

Eisner argued in 1967 that behavioural objectives overestimate how far outcomes can be predicted, favour subject matter that reduces easily to specifiable behaviour, confuse applying a standard with exercising judgment, and wrongly treat objective-setting as the necessary first step in planning; he proposed the expressive objective, which names an encounter and leaves its outcome open, as a complement rather than a replacement.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the cognitive categories form a genuine cumulative hierarchy in which mastery of each level requires the level below.
positions: The 1956 handbook assumed a cumulative hierarchy in which achievement of a more complex category required achievement of the prior one.

Krathwohl (2002) reports that the revision relaxed the strict-hierarchy requirement to allow overlap, and hedges that the revised ordering would 'probably' be supported about as well as the original was - a comparative statement, not an endorsement.
Heer's Iowa State model states that the distinctions between categories are not always clear-cut, giving an example where analysing or evaluating may be no less complex than creating.
Larsen et al. (2022) found the two dimensions are not independent and that prompt verbs do not track cognitive processes cleanly.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the ordering as a rough complexity gradient that is useful for aiming an objective, states plainly that the cumulative hierarchy was an assumption rather than a demonstrated result, and warns against using a verb list as if it certified a level. It does not claim the hierarchy has been refuted, only that it was never established in the strong form popular summaries assert.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether every objective needs a stated condition and a numeric degree.
positions: Mager's format and the ABCD elaboration present condition and criterion as components of a complete objective.
NYSED itself notes conditions may be omitted when they follow from the instruction, and that percentage criteria are inappropriate for some tasks.
Eisner argued the full specification burden is impractical and distorting at classroom scale.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the components, then teaches a rule for when each earns its place: state the condition when it changes the difficulty of the task, state the degree when a real threshold exists. It presents over-specification as a recognised failure mode rather than as rigour.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's entire body was placeholder text with no factual content about learning objectives; nothing in it was source-supported.

The draft's In 30 Seconds, Why This Matters, College Version, vocabulary, worked example, common mistakes and all three quick-check questions were generic templates naming the topic but teaching nothing about it.
The draft's analogy ('a label on a toolbox drawer') and its second analogy ('reading a map legend') were topic-agnostic filler and carried no analogy limits.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire generated draft with researched content; retained only the topic identity, slug and title.
Added the historical record for the 1956 handbook, including the full committee authorship and the examination-classification purpose, which the draft did not mention.

Stated explicitly that the cumulative hierarchy was assumed rather than demonstrated and that the 2001 revision relaxed it, rather than presenting Bloom's levels as an established developmental sequence.
Added the empirical caution that action verbs do not reliably indicate cognitive level, so that the lesson does not teach verb-list shopping as a method.
Added Eisner's critique so that objective-writing is presented as a contested practice with real limits rather than as settled orthodoxy.
Built all verb and objective examples from scratch rather than adapting any published verb table.
rightsIssues: The Heer / Iowa State model is CC BY-NC-SA 3.0. Its verb and knowledge-type tables were deliberately not reproduced or adapted; only the general verb-plus-object formulation and the source's own caveat about category overlap were used, with attribution.

Mager (1962), the 1956 and 1964 handbooks, the 2001 revision, and Biggs (1996) are all in-copyright works cited bibliographically; no text from any of them appears in the lesson.

sourceRecords.title: A Revision of Bloom's Taxonomy: An Overview
sourceRecords.provider: David R. Krathwohl, Syracuse University; Theory Into Practice 41(4), 212-218, Autumn 2002 (College of Education, The Ohio State University); scanned issue hosted by IHMC CmapTools public server
sourceRecords.notes: Primary source for the history and structure of both taxonomies. Read in full text. Confirms: Bloom, then associate director of the Board of Examinations at the University of Chicago, initiated the project to reduce the labour of preparing annual comprehensive examinations; the group of measurement specialists met about twice a year from 1949; the 1956 Handbook I authorship (Bloom ed., Engelhart, Furst, Hill, Krathwohl); the affective domain Handbook II (Krathwohl, Bloom & Masia, 1964); that no psychomotor taxonomy was ever published by the originating group (Simpson 1966, Dave 1970, Harrow 1972 published their own); the original six categories and the statement that a cumulative hierarchy was assumed; the 2001 revision's six cognitive process categories, the four knowledge types, the Taxonomy Table, and the explicit statement that 'the requirement of a strict hierarchy has been relaxed to allow the categories to overlap one another', illustrated by Explaining (Understand) being more complex than Executing (Apply). No source wording reproduced in the lesson beyond short attributed characterisations.

sourceRecords.title: Curricular Alignment: A Re-Examination
sourceRecords.provider: Lorin W. Anderson, University of South Carolina; Theory Into Practice 41(4), Autumn 2002 (College of Education, The Ohio State University); same scanned issue as the Krathwohl overview
sourceRecords.notes: Article appearing later in the same scanned Theory Into Practice issue (deliberately given the same URL as the Krathwohl record, which is a scan of the whole issue). Supports the three-component alignment triangle (objectives/standards, instructional activities and materials, assessments) and the distinction between content coverage ('Is what we are teaching being tested?') and opportunity to learn ('Are we teaching what is being tested?'). Used only for that conceptual distinction; no wording reproduced. [URL corrected to canonical Theory Into Practice DOI; prior value was a mispaste of the Krathwohl PDF link.]

sourceRecords.title: Probing Internal Assumptions of the Revised Bloom's Taxonomy
sourceRecords.provider: Tori M. Larsen, Bianca H. Endo, Alexander T. Yee, Tony Do, Stanley M. Lo; CBE-Life Sciences Education 21(4), ar66 (2022); DOI 10.1187/cbe.20-08-0170; PMID 36112622; PubMed Central PMC9727608
sourceRecords.notes: Empirical test of two assumptions built into the revised taxonomy; read via the PubMed Central full text, where the license statement appears. Supports the two claims used in the lesson: contingency analysis of 940 assessment items found the knowledge-type and cognitive-process dimensions are related rather than independent (Fisher's exact test, p < 0.0001), and analysis using the Shannon evenness index found no reliable relationship between question prompt words, action verbs included, and the cognitive processes actually embedded in the items - so verbs alone are not sufficient to classify an objective's level. The publisher site (lifescied.org) returns HTTP 403 to automated requests; the PMC mirror was used instead. No wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: A Model of Learning Objectives based on A Taxonomy for Learning, Teaching, and Assessing: A Revision of Bloom's Taxonomy of Educational Objectives
sourceRecords.provider: Rex Heer, Center for Excellence in Learning and Teaching, Iowa State University (updated January 2012); copy hosted by the University of Central Florida Office of Effectiveness and Accreditation Support
sourceRecords.notes: Widely used two-dimensional model of the revised taxonomy, with the license statement printed on the document itself. Supports the verb-plus-object structure of an objective (the verb names the intended cognitive process, the object names the knowledge to be acquired or constructed) and the document's own caveat that the distinctions between categories are not always clear-cut - an objective involving analysing or evaluating may demand thinking no less complex than one involving creating. Its verb and knowledge-type tables were NOT reproduced; all verb examples in the lesson are original.

sourceRecords.title: Writing Performance Objectives
sourceRecords.provider: New York State Education Department, Adult Career and Continuing Education Services / Bureau of Proprietary School Supervision
sourceRecords.notes: State education agency guidance. Supports the three-component structure (student performance, conditions, criterion); the explicit rejection of verbs such as 'learn', 'understand' and 'become familiar with' on the ground that a teacher cannot observe a student understanding; the definition of conditions as the equipment or material required for the demonstration, and the note that conditions can be omitted when they follow from instruction alone; and the warning that vague standards such as 'to the satisfaction of the instructor' are unusable and that a fixed percentage criterion is inappropriate for tasks where partial accuracy is unacceptable. Page carries a NYSED copyright notice; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Preparing Instructional Objectives (ERIC record ED018143)
sourceRecords.provider: Robert F. Mager (Fearon Publishers, 1962); record hosted by ERIC, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education
sourceRecords.notes: Bibliographic anchor for the 1962 publication that established the performance/conditions/criterion format for instructional objectives. Used for attribution and date only; the three-component account taught in the lesson is corroborated by the NYSED guidance record. The book itself is in copyright and was not reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Instructional and Expressive Educational Objectives: Their Formulation and Use in Curriculum (ERIC record ED028838)
sourceRecords.provider: Elliot W. Eisner, 1967; record and full text hosted by ERIC, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education
sourceRecords.notes: Primary source for the standing critique of the behavioural-objectives movement. Full text read via the ERIC document scan. Supports: that educational outcomes cannot be predicted with the certainty the behavioural-objectives model assumes; that specification favours subject matter which reduces easily to stated behaviours over creative or imaginative work; that objectives supply standards but standards do not substitute for judgment; that treating objective-setting as the necessary first planning step confuses logical with psychological order; the sheer arithmetic of specifying objectives for every unit of content; and the definition of an expressive objective as a named encounter whose outcome is left open and evaluated afterwards. Eisner argued for using both kinds of objective, not for abandoning objectives. No wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Enhancing Teaching through Constructive Alignment (ERIC record EJ534311)
sourceRecords.provider: John Biggs, Higher Education 32(3), 347-364, October 1996; record hosted by ERIC, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education
sourceRecords.notes: Bibliographic record and abstract for the paper that named constructive alignment. Supports the attribution, date and journal details, and the abstract's description of the framework guiding decisions at every stage of instructional design: deriving objectives as performances at a suitable cognitive level, choosing teaching and learning activities judged to elicit those performances, and assessing and reporting the same performances. Article is behind a publisher paywall; only the ERIC abstract was read, and nothing was reproduced.
